passage:
My name is Jagdish, and I still remember the envelope. It was addressed to my wife, Afreen, but it had the bank's name in the window, so I opened it thinking it was about our joint account. It wasn't. It was a reminder for a loan of four lakh rupees, in her name, taken eight months earlier. I read it three times standing by the shoe rack.
When she came home, I just held it up. She went pale and said, "It was for Imran's shop. I was going to tell you."
Eight months. I had sat beside her at her brother's shop opening and clapped. I felt like the only person in the room who hadn't been told the joke.
That night I lay awake going through everything: the phone she said was a gift, the late evenings, the savings figure she always rounded off. What else?

qa.q: What did Afreen say the loan was for?
qa.a: Afreen said it was for Imran's shop.

qa.q: What does Jagdish's sleepless night suggest he is thinking?
qa.a: Jagdish has started doubting everything, going back over the phone, the late evenings and the savings figure and wondering what else Afreen has hidden.

qa.q: At this first stage, what could help Jagdish before the next talk with Afreen?
qa.a: Jagdish could take a little time for the shock to settle, then ask Afreen for the whole story calmly instead of piecing it together alone at night. Talking to a trusted friend or a counsellor could also help.

qa.q: What might Afreen be going through when Jagdish holds up the letter?
qa.a: Afreen is likely frightened and ashamed, caught between protecting her brother and facing her husband. Going pale and saying 'I was going to tell you' suggests she knew this moment would come.

grounding: Shows a husband discovering his wife's hidden loan for her brother, with shock, a sense of being made a fool, and sudden doubt about other secrets.

Note for file, Tuesday. Siddharth, shift supervisor.
Around eleven, Manoj took a call at his desk and went very still. He asked the caller to repeat the amount twice and wrote nothing down. Then he stepped into the corridor and phoned his wife. I heard, "For Rakesh? Your brother's shop? Eight months and you said nothing?"
When he came back he stared at his screen without typing for almost twenty minutes. Then he asked me, quite seriously, whether there was any way to check if other loans had his address on them. He laughed once, not a happy laugh: "Last to know in my own house."
His hand shook when he picked up his water bottle.
I did not ask for details. I told him to take the afternoon off, reminded him the staff counselling line is free and private, and said the report could wait. He left at one. I will check in with him quietly tomorrow.

qa.q: How long did Manoj stare at his screen without typing?
qa.a: Manoj stared at his screen without typing for almost twenty minutes.

qa.q: What does Manoj's question about other loans suggest he is worried about?
qa.a: It suggests Manoj suddenly fears there may be more hidden debts; one secret has made him doubt what else he does not know.

qa.q: How did Siddharth support Manoj at this stage, and what else could help?
qa.a: Siddharth gave Manoj the afternoon off, mentioned the free, private counselling line and did not pry. Once the first shock passes, a calm talk with his wife, perhaps with a counsellor, could be a next step.

qa.q: How might Manoj's wife be feeling after his call?
qa.a: She is probably scared and ashamed now that the secret is out, and may be bracing for his anger while still worried about her brother Rakesh.

grounding: Illustrates the moment a husband learns of a large loan his wife took for her brother, and his shock, humiliation and doubt, as seen by his supervisor.

12 March, night
Prashant found the loan papers today. He didn't shout, which was worse. He just asked, "Why?" and I heard myself say, "Because you would never have agreed." His face closed like a door. I meant it as the truth, but it came out as if I was blaming him for my lie.
The truth is messier. When Sharmila bhabhi called crying that the landlord would shut Bhaiya's shop, I thought of Papa telling us as kids that a sister never counts favours for her brother. And then I thought of Prashant's face last year when my cousin borrowed money, and the long lecture after. So I signed, and every month I paid it from my salary and said nothing.
I'm ashamed. I'm also angry that I felt I had to hide it. Both are true tonight.
Mahima

qa.a: Mahima said, 'Because you would never have agreed.'

qa.q: What mixed feelings is Mahima writing about at the end of the entry?
qa.a: Mahima feels ashamed of hiding the loan and also angry that she felt she had to hide it; she writes that both are true tonight.

qa.a: Mahima could go back and say plainly that hiding it was wrong, without 'you would never have agreed', and then explain her fear and her brother's trouble as context, not as an excuse.

qa.q: How might Prashant have heard Mahima's answer?
qa.a: Prashant likely heard it as blame, as if his temper caused her secret, which made the hurt worse; that is why his face 'closed like a door'.

grounding: Shows the wife torn between family loyalty and fear of her husband's reaction, and how her defence that he would never have agreed deepens his hurt.

Sahil,
I'm writing this because when I try to say it aloud, we both get tight in the throat.
I see you open the bank app every morning before you've even had tea. I see you study my face when my phone buzzes, as if you're reading a weather report. Last night you asked who "P" was in my messages. It was the plumber.
I understand why. After what I hid, your mind is trying to make sure you never get hit like that again. I don't blame you for it.
But I also see how tired you are. You aren't sleeping. And I feel like I'm living with an auditor, not a husband who is trying to forgive me. I don't know how long either of us can keep this up.
Could we find another way, together? I'll show you anything you ask. I'm your wife, not a suspect. I just want to be asked, not watched.

passage:
Thursday, late
Tonight I told Lokesh everything. Not the version I'd been editing in my head for weeks. All of it. Twelve years his wife and I'd never written him anything this long.
The loan for my brother Gurnam's truck, yes, but also the second, smaller one from Chachi's friend when the first repayment fell short, and the gold bangles I pawned in March. I wrote it all on one page so I wouldn't lose my nerve halfway.
I said, "Hiding this was wrong. Not your temper, not Gurnam's trouble. My choice." My voice shook on "my choice".
He didn't say it was okay. He read the page twice and asked, "Is this all?" I said yes, and for the first time in months it was actually true.
Some numbers I wasn't sure of, and I said so instead of guessing.
We didn't fix anything. But there is nothing left under the carpet.
Baljeet

qa.a: Baljeet pawned the gold bangles in March.

qa.a: Baljeet felt nervous and exposed; her voice shook on 'my choice', yet she still said it.

qa.a: It let Baljeet give one complete account instead of facts trickling out later, which is what lets rebuilding begin; saying she wasn't sure of some numbers kept it honest.

qa.a: Lokesh is probably bracing for more surprises; reading the page twice and asking shows he needs to know the ground is finally solid before trust can start again.

Sunday
Our first "money Sunday". Kunal made chai, I opened the shared sheet, and we went through the month line by line, his side and mine. He had to explain a cricket bat he'd bought for his nephew and actually blushed. That helped more than he knows. It wasn't just me on trial.
Then my cousin Deepika texted asking if I could lend her something for her course fees. Old me would have sent it and deleted the message. Instead I showed Kunal, and we used the rule we agreed with the counsellor: any family help beyond small things, we talk first and decide together, even when the answer is yes. The answer was yes.
Kunal joked that his wife now keeps better records than his office. We've said we'll keep this Sunday habit for six months and then see if we still need it. It feels less like a cage than I feared. More like a handrail.
Trisha

The staff canteen at the district hospital is loud at one o'clock, but Nirmala, his friend since their nursing college days, could still tell when Gurpreet wasn't really listening. For a month he'd been easier: laughing at the ward jokes, showing her photos of the Sunday picnic with his wife Harleen and the kids. Today he was pushing his rajma around and not eating it.

"Harleen's cousin came by with sweets to celebrate his new shop," he said. "Just sweets. And I thought of the loan and couldn't breathe for a second. I thought we were past it."

"Then maybe see the counsellor on the second floor, both of you," she said. "Someone who can keep the conversation steady."

Come, sit. You're sulking because Riddhi played with the new girl, na? Let me tell you about your Nani and Amandeep.
We were ten, in Ludhiana. Every afternoon we walked home together along the canal, and we had a code: if one of us tugged an earlobe, it meant "meet at the neem tree after tea." We scratched our initials into its bark. She said, "You are my best friend, Chandrika, forever," and I felt as if the sky belonged to me.
Then one day at recess she skipped rope with Kamaljit's group. Just once. I went home and refused dinner. I told my mother Amandeep was a traitor.
Next morning she tugged her ear at me in the assembly line, as if nothing had happened. And for her, nothing had.
It hurt, beta, and it was also a little silly. Both.

Every lunch break, Mrs Kurian stood on duty near the art room steps, where she could see the whole playground. In June, Thomas and Chinmay still sat together with one sketchbook between them, drawing robots.
By August, Thomas had been picked for the under-eleven football team. Now at the bell he sprinted straight to the field, boots knocking against his bag. Chinmay went up the art room steps, where a group was painting a mural of the school garden.
Some days Thomas glanced at the steps before running off. Once Chinmay waved a paintbrush when Thomas scored a goal.
Mrs Kurian thought about calling them in for a talk, then didn't. There was no fight to fix. In the staffroom she told a colleague, "They haven't fallen out. They've just grown in different directions this term."

qa.q: Which team was Thomas picked for?
qa.a: Thomas was picked for the under-eleven football team.

qa.q: What might Thomas's glance at the steps suggest he is thinking?
qa.a: It suggests Thomas still thinks about Chinmay and may feel a small pull between the old friend and the new team.

qa.q: Why was Mrs Kurian wise not to call them in for a talk?
qa.a: No one had done anything wrong, so a talk might have made them feel they had failed; watching quietly lets the change happen naturally.

qa.q: How might Chinmay feel about Thomas running to the field every day?
qa.a: Chinmay may miss the robot drawings a little but also enjoys the mural group, and the paintbrush wave shows there is still warmth.

grounding: Shows a teacher noticing two friends drifting into football and art groups with no one at fault.

passage:
I've taught Karthik and Sabina since Class 3, and last year you couldn't separate them. They shared a tiffin, a pencil sharpener, even a cold, I think.
This term I've watched something shift. Karthik stays after school for football practice now; I see him in the corridor with mud up to his knees, talking goals with four other boys. Sabina has joined the art club and spends lunch in the art room with Esther and Pooja, making clay birds for the annual day.
I don't think anything happened between them. I haven't seen a quarrel, no sulking at each other's desks. When Karthik scored in the inter-house match, Sabina clapped from the art room window. I can't say what either of them feels. Maybe they miss each other, maybe not yet. It looks to me as if their days simply went different ways.

qa.q: What is Sabina making in the art room?
qa.a: Sabina is making clay birds for the annual day with Esther and Pooja.

qa.q: Why does the teacher say 'I can't say what either of them feels'?
qa.a: The teacher only sees what the children do, not what's inside; the teacher thinks there was no quarrel but can't be sure whether Karthik and Sabina miss each other.

qa.q: How could the teacher support both children through this change?
qa.a: The teacher could leave the new groups alone while offering small chances to mix, like a class project, so the old friendship stays kind without being forced.

qa.q: What would change if the teacher had seen a quarrel?
qa.a: Then there might be hurt to help them repair; without one, it is just new activities pulling them apart, and no one needs to be blamed.

grounding: Illustrates a teacher observing two former close friends moving into football and art circles without any wrongdoing.
